abstract: Independent Component Analysis (ICA) was introduced in the 1980's as a model for Blind Source Separation (BSS), which refers to the process of recovering the sources underlying a mixture of signals, with little knowledge about the source signals or the mixing process. While there are many sophisticated algorithms for estimation, different methods have different shortcomings. In this paper, we develop a nonparametric score to adaptively pick the right algorithm for ICA with arbitrary Gaussian noise. The novelty of this score stems from the fact that it just assumes a finite second moment of the data and uses the characteristic function to evaluate the quality of the estimated mixing matrix without any knowledge of the parameters of the noise distribution. In addition, we propose some new contrast functions and algorithms that enjoy the same fast computability as existing algorithms like FASTICA and JADE but work in domains where the former may fail. While these also may have weaknesses, our proposed diagnostic, as shown by our simulations, can remedy them. Finally, we propose a theoretical framework to analyze the local and global convergence properties of our algorithms.

# Keep or toss?

# A nonparametric score to evaluate solutions for noisy ICA

Syamantak Kumar\*, Purnamrita Sarkar  $\dagger 2$  , Peter Bickel  $\ddagger 3$  , and Derek Bean  $\S 4$

$^{1}$ Department of Computer Science, University of Texas at Austin  
 $^{2}$ Department of Statistics and Data Sciences, University of Texas at Austin  
 $^{3}$ Department of Statistics, University of California, Berkeley  
 $^{4}$ Department of Statistics, University of Wisconsin, Madison

# Abstract

Independent Component Analysis (ICA) was introduced in the 1980's as a model for Blind Source Separation (BSS), which refers to the process of recovering the sources underlying a mixture of signals, with little knowledge about the source signals or the mixing process. While there are many sophisticated algorithms for estimation, different methods have different shortcomings. In this paper, we develop a nonparametric score to adaptively pick the right algorithm for ICA with arbitrary Gaussian noise. The novelty of this score stems from the fact that it just assumes a finite second moment of the data and uses the characteristic function to evaluate the quality of the estimated mixing matrix without any knowledge of the parameters of the noise distribution. In addition, we propose some new contrast functions and algorithms that enjoy the same fast computability as existing algorithms like FASTICA and JADE but work in domains where the former may fail. While these also may have weaknesses, our proposed diagnostic, as shown by our simulations, can remedy them. Finally, we propose a theoretical framework to analyze the local and global convergence properties of our algorithms.

# 1 Introduction

Independent Component Analysis (ICA) was introduced in the 1980's as a model for Blind Source Separation (BSS) [11, 10], which refers to the process of recovering the sources underlying a mixture of signals, with little knowledge about the source signals or the mixing process. It has become a powerful alternative to the Gaussian model leading to PCA in factor analysis. A good account of the history and many results are in [21]. In one of its first forms, ICA is based on observing  $n$  independent samples from a  $k$ -dimensional population:

$$
\boldsymbol {x} = B \boldsymbol {z} + \boldsymbol {g} \tag {1}
$$

where  $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$  ( $d \geq k$ ) is an unknown mixing matrix,  $\pmb{z} \in \mathbb{R}^k$  is a vector of statistically independent mean zero "sources" or "factors" and  $\pmb{g} \sim N(\pmb{0}, \Sigma)$  is a  $d$  dimensional mean zero Gaussian noise vector with covariance matrix  $\Sigma$ , independent of  $\pmb{z}$ . We denote  $\operatorname{diag}(\pmb{a}) \coloneqq \operatorname{cov}(\pmb{z})$  and  $S \coloneqq \operatorname{cov}(\pmb{x}) = B \operatorname{diag}(\pmb{a}) B^T + \Sigma$ . The goal of the problem is to estimate  $B$ .

ICA was initially developed in the context of  $\pmb{g} = 0$ , now called noiseless ICA. In that form, it spawned an enormous literature [14, 27, 28, 1, 6, 20, 24, 26, 17, 9] and at least two well-established algorithms FASTICA [22] and JADE [7] which are widely used. The general model with nonzero  $\pmb{g}$  and unknown noise covariance matrix  $\Sigma$ , known as noisy ICA, has developed more slowly, with its own literature [4, 33, 32]. As we will show in the coming sections, the many different methods and objective functions of ICA and noisy

ICA suffer from different shortcomings. Some work poorly for heavy-tailed source distributions and outliers, whereas others require estimation of the marginal density, which is computationally hard. Methods for the noiseless case may work well in the noisy setting [32], but not always. See Figure 1 in [32] and Theorem 2 in [9]. Despite this plethora of algorithms for noisy and noiseless ICA, what has been largely missing in the literature is a diagnostic to decide which algorithm to pick for a given dataset. This is our main goal. In this paper our contribution is twofold. First, we propose a diagnostic that can be used to pick the best algorithm from a set of candidate algorithms. Second, we propose some methods for noisy ICA that only require bounded second moments. These, as we will show have their own difficulties, possibly complementary to the problems of the existing methods, which our diagnostic can remedy.

Notation: We denote vectors using bold font as  $\pmb{v} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ . The dataset is represented as  $\{\pmb{x}^{(i)}\}_{i \in [n]}$  for  $\pmb{x}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ . Scalars and matrices are represented using lower case and upper case letters, respectively, as  $s \in \mathbb{R}$  and  $M \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times q}$ .  $\pmb{I}_k$  denotes the  $k-$  dimensional identity matrix. Entries of vector  $\pmb{v}$  are represented as  $v_i$ , and entries of matrix,  $M$ , are represented as  $M_{i,j}$ .  $M(:, i)$  represents the  $i^{\text{th}}$  column and  $M(i,:)$  represents the  $i^{\text{th}}$  row of matrix  $M$ .  $M^\dagger$  represents the Moore-Penrose inverse of  $M$ .  $\|\cdot\|$  represents the Euclidean  $l_2$  norm for vectors and operator norm for matrices.  $\|\cdot\|_F$  similarly represents the Frobenius norm for matrices.  $\mathbb{E}[.]$  denotes the expectation operator and  $\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[.]$  denotes the empirical average. We will use  $\pmb{x} \perp \pmb{y}$  to denote statistical independence. Later, for suitable choices of functions  $g$ , we will introduce contrast functions,  $f$ , denoted by  $f(\pmb{u}|P) \equiv f(\pmb{u}|\pmb{x}) = \mathbb{E}_{\pmb{x} \sim P}[g(\pmb{u}^T\pmb{x})]$  for any random variable  $\pmb{x}$  generated from distribution  $P$ .

# 2 Background and Overview

In this section, we provide a general overview of the main concepts behind the evolution of the area of ICA. We start with the important topic of identifiability.

Identifiability: The key issue in these models is the identifiability of  $A \coloneqq B^{-1}$ , which holds up to permutation and scaling of the coordinates of  $z$  if, at most, one component of  $z$  is Gaussian. This is closely related to the Darmois-Skitovich theorem [12, 30]. A version of this result summarizing other previous research can be found in [13]. If  $d = k$  and  $\Sigma$  are unknown, it is possible, as we shall see later, to identify the canonical versions  $B$  and  $\Sigma$ . If  $d > k$  and  $\Sigma$  is unknown, it is possible (see [13]) to identify  $k$  and  $d - k$  dimensional subspaces corresponding to  $M(z + g^{(1)}) \in \mathbb{R}^k$  and  $g^{(2)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d - k}$ , where  $g^{(1)}, g^{(2)}$  are independent Gaussians. Thus, the  $d > k$  case reduces to the  $d = k$  case. In this work, we assume  $d = k$ .

A version with  $d > k$ , and  $z$  could be Gaussian has long been present under the name "Factor Analysis". This arose in the context of psychometrics where  $z$  represented "important" independent factors. An interesting recent paper [29] gives this background and gives some new contributions. For factor models, when  $z$  is Gaussian, identifiability only holds up to an orthogonal transformation in addition to scaling of individual components. Thus, the factors are only identifiable up to rotation and scaling, leading to the non-interpretability of classical factor models. This suggests fitting strategies focusing on recovering  $C$  through nongaussianity as well as independence. In classical work on ICA, a large class of algorithms (see [26]) choose to optimize a measure of non-gaussianity.

Contrast functions: Formally, we define a contrast function  $f(\boldsymbol{u}|P)$  by  $f:\mathcal{B}_k\times \mathcal{P}\to \mathbb{R}$  where  $\mathcal{B}_k$  is the unit ball in  $\mathbb{R}^k$  and  $\mathcal{P}$  is essentially the class of mean zero distributions on  $\mathbb{R}^d$ . The most popular example of a contrast function is the kurtosis, which is defined as,  $f(\boldsymbol {u}|P) = E_{\boldsymbol{x}\sim P}\left[\frac{(\boldsymbol{u}^T\boldsymbol{x})^4}{E[(\boldsymbol{u}^T\boldsymbol{x})^2]^2}\right] - 3$ . The idea is to construct an estimate  $\hat{f} (\pmb {u})$  and maximize  $\hat{f} (\pmb {u})$ . Notable contrast functions are the negentropy, mutual information (used by the INFOMAX algorithm [5]), the tanh function, etc. (See [26] for further details).

Fitting strategies: The existing fitting strategies fall into two broad categories. (I) Find  $A$  such that the components of  $Ax$  are both as nongaussian and as independent as possible. The chief representative of this class is JADE [7], based on multivariate kurtosis. Another, figuring largely in our work is the characteristic function-based methods of [16] and [9]. The latter we shall call the PFICA method. (II) Find successively the  $j^{th}$  row of  $A$ , denoted by  $A(j,:) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ ,  $j = 1,\dots,k$  such that  $A(j,:)^T\pmb{x}$  are independent and each as nongaussian as possible, that is, estimate  $A(1,:)$ , project, and then apply the method again on the residuals successively. The chief representative of these methods is FastICA [20] based on univariate kurtosis.

From noiseless to noisy ICA: In the noiseless case one can first transform  $\pmb{x}^{(1)},\dots,\pmb{x}^{(n)}$  to  $\tilde{\pmb{x}}^{(1)},\dots,\tilde{\pmb{x}}^{(n)}$  where  $\tilde{\pmb{x}}\gets \hat{\Sigma}^{-1 / 2}\pmb {x}$ , where  $\hat{\Sigma}$  is the empirical variance-covariance matrix of the  $\pmb{x}^{(i)}$ . This immediately allows one to assume that  $B$  is orthogonal without loss of generality. Searching over orthogonal matrices not only satisfies algorithm design for fitting strategy (I) but also makes strategy (II) meaningful. As we will show in detail later, it simplifies the analysis of kurtosis-based contrast functions [15].

However, prewhitening is challenging for noisy ICA because the covariance matrix of the data includes that of the Gaussian noise, which is typically unknown. Of many excellent approaches that attempt to overcome this problem, we highlight the ones most related to our work, beginning with [4]. There, the authors show that it is enough to quasi orthogonalize the data, i.e. multiply it by a matrix which makes the data have a diagonal covariance matrix (not necessarily the identity). Subsequent work [32, 33] uses cumulants to create a  $C$  matrix of the form  $BDB^T$ , and then use this matrix to achieve quasi-orthogonalization. However, a difficulty is that  $D$  may not be positive semidefinite (PSD)-for example, when the signal mixes positive and negative kurtosis random variables. In an earlier paper [33], Voss et al. propose a method to learn a  $C$  that is PSD. However, their later work [32] foregoes this step via a novel iterative power method, where the updates use  $C$  in such a way that implicitly, the optimization happens in a pseudo-Euclidean space. Their method extracts one column of  $B$  at a time.

Note that if we are optimizing the contrast function  $f(\pmb{u} | P)$  with a constraint of  $\| \pmb{u} \| = 1$ , then using the lagrangian multiplier method, we have for the optimum  $\pmb{u}_{\mathrm{opt}}$ ,  $\pmb{u}_{\mathrm{opt}} = \frac{\nabla f(\pmb{u}_{\mathrm{opt}} | P)}{\|\nabla f(\pmb{u}_{\mathrm{opt}} | P)\|}$ . This leads to a natural fixed-point algorithm for computing  $\pmb{u}_{\mathrm{opt}}$  which, given an initialisation  $\pmb{u}_0$ , proceeds as  $\pmb{u}_t \gets \frac{\nabla f(\pmb{u}_{t-1} | P)}{\|\nabla f(\pmb{u}_{t-1} | P)\|}$ . The beauty of the power method in the pseudo-Euclidean space, proposed in [32], is that one first computes a matrix  $C$ , which is typically the Hessian of  $f(\pmb{u})$  evaluated at some fixed unit vectors. Then, instead of doing a prewhitening at the beginning, the idea is to do it implicitly in the power iteration -

$$
\boldsymbol {u} _ {t} \leftarrow \frac {\nabla f \left(C ^ {\dagger} \boldsymbol {u} _ {t - 1} | P\right)}{\| \nabla f \left(C ^ {\dagger} \boldsymbol {u} _ {t - 1} | P\right) \|} \tag {2}
$$

# Desirable properties of contrast functions:

1. If  $\hat{\pmb{u}} = \arg \max |\hat{f} (\pmb {u})|$  and  $\pmb {u}(P) = \arg \max |\hat{f} (\pmb {u})|$ , then  $\hat{\pmb{u}}\stackrel {P}{\to}\pmb {u}(P)$ .  
2.  $f(\pmb{u}|\pmb{z}) = 0$  for  $\pmb{z}$  mean zero Gaussian.  
3. Write  $f(\pmb{u}|\pmb{x})$  for  $\pmb{x} \sim P$ . If  $\pmb{x}^{(1)}$  and  $\pmb{x}^{(2)}$  are independent,  $\mathbb{E}\left[\pmb{x}^{(i)}\right] = 0$ ,  $\operatorname{var}(\pmb{x}^{(i)}) = 1$ , then, if  $a^2 + b^2 = 1$ ,  $|f(\pmb{u}|a\pmb{x}^{(1)} + b\pmb{x}^{(2)})| \leq \max_j |f(\pmb{u}|\pmb{x}^{(j)})|$ .  
4.  $f(\boldsymbol{u}|\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{z}) = f(\boldsymbol{u}|\boldsymbol{x})$  if  $\boldsymbol{z}, \boldsymbol{x}$  are independent mean zero random vectors and  $\boldsymbol{z}$  is Gaussian.

Recall that the  $r^{th}$  cumulant of a random variable  $X$  is the coefficient of  $u^r$  in the expansion of  $\log \mathbb{E}[\exp (uX)]$ . Cumulants satisfy properties 1-4. [15] establish property 3 for kurtosis. In fact, their argument naturally generalizes to other cumulants. If valid, properties 1-3 guarantee that  $\hat{\pmb{u}}$  is a consistent estimate of a maximal direction in the noiseless case, which corresponds to a scalar multiple of a single independent  $(z)$  component.

Individual shortcomings of different contrast functions: Unfortunately, all contrast functions fail to obey some of these conditions. Kurtosis and even cumulants can vanish for non-Gaussian distributions, which makes property 3 vacuous. Our experiments suggest that even the presence of a few independent components with zero kurtosis can derail the behavior of kurtosis-based contrast functions. On the other hand, cumulant-based contrast functions are not defined if higher moments do not exist and it is well known [3, 9, 19] that in practice, using contrast functions depending on higher order moments is preferable. Even if contrast functions do not obey property 3, they may still, under suitable conditions, converge to maximal directions. We introduce one such contrast function which vanishes iff  $\pmb{x}$  is Gaussian in Section 4 and does not require higher moments.

Contrast functions involving entropy require estimation of the probability density functions and typically simpler moment-based approximations are used [26], which have their own shortcomings.

As we will see, PFICA works in situations where algorithms like FASTICA, JADE, and pseudo-euclidean iteration-based methods do not perform well. However, it is computationally much slower than the later methods. It also does not work well for Bernoulli  $(p)$  random variables with very small  $p$ . Thus, even though

these algorithms work well in most situations, there are many competitors that work better under some circumstances. Determining an algorithm that "always" works is a problem. Our contributions are:

1. Using Theorem 1 to obtain a scoring method for choosing between different algorithms, without sacrificing the speed too much. Our score can also be applied to choose and evaluate each demixing direction in sequential settings. However, we do not pursue this here.  
2. Proposing new contrast functions with well-defined domains that work under scenarios where cumulant-based methods fail. In doing so, we extend the one-at-a-time approach of [32].

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 contains background and notation. Section 3.1 contains the independence score, its properties, and a Meta algorithm 1 that utilizes this score. Section 5 presents the global and local convergence results for noisy ICA. Section 4 introduces new contrast functions based on the natural logarithm of the characteristic function and moment generating function of  $\pmb{x}^T\pmb{u}$ . Section 6 demonstrates the empirical performance of our new contrast functions as well as the Meta algorithm applied to a variety of methods for inferring  $B$ .

# 3 A Nonparametric Independence Score

In this section, we present the "Independence score" and state the key result that justifies it.

# 3.1 Independence score

Let us start with noiseless ICA to build intuition. Say we have estimated the inverse of the mixing matrix, i.e.  $B^{-1}$  using a matrix  $F$ . Ideally, if  $F = B^{-1}$ , then  $F\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{z}$ , where  $\mathbf{z}$  is a vector of independent random variables. Kac's theorem [23] tells us that  $\mathbb{E}\left[\exp (it^T\mathbf{z})\right] = \prod_{j = 1}^{k}\mathbb{E}\left[\exp (it_jz_j)\right]$  if and only if  $z_{i}$  are independent.

In [16], a novel characteristic function-based objective (CHFICA), is further analyzed and studied by [9] (PFICA). Here one minimizes  $\left| \mathbb{E}\left[\exp (it^T F\pmb {x})\right] - \prod_{j = 1}^{k}\mathbb{E}\left[\exp (it_j(F\pmb {x})_j)\right] \right|$  over  $F$ . We refer to this objective as the uncorrected independence score. We propose to adapt the CHFICA objective using estimable parameters to the noisy ICA setting. We will minimize the following quantity.

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Delta (\boldsymbol {t}, F | P) = \left| \underbrace {\mathbb {E} \left[ \exp (i \boldsymbol {t} ^ {T} F \boldsymbol {x}) \right] \exp \left(- \frac {\boldsymbol {t} ^ {T} \operatorname {d i a g} (F S F ^ {T}) \boldsymbol {t}}{2}\right)} _ {L. H. S} \right. \\ - \underbrace {\prod_ {j = 1} ^ {k} \mathbb {E} \left[ \exp \left(i t _ {j} \left(F \boldsymbol {x}\right) _ {j}\right) \right] \exp \left(- \frac {\boldsymbol {t} ^ {T} F S F ^ {T} \boldsymbol {t}}{2}\right)} _ {R. H. S} \tag {3} \\ \end{array}
$$

where  $S$  is the covariance matrix of the data and can be estimated using the sample covariance matrix of the data, and hence does not require knowledge of any model parameters.

We refer to this score as the (corrected) independence score. The novelty of this score is that it ingeniously uses the form of the characteristic function of a Gaussian random variable. In the proof sketch, we build intuition with a small toy example. See [16] for a related score requiring knowledge of the unknown Gaussian covariance matrix  $\Sigma$ . We are now ready to present our first theoretical result.

Theorem 1. Recall the independence score  $\Delta (\pmb {t},F|P)$  defined in Eq 3. If  $F$  is invertible, then  $\Delta (\pmb {t},F|P) = 0$  iff  $F = DB^{-1}$  where  $D$  is a permutation of an arbitrary diagonal matrix.

The proof of Theorem 1 is provided in the Appendix Section A.1. When using this score in practice,  $S$  is replaced with the sample covariance matrix of the data, and the expectations are replaced by the empirical estimates of the characteristic function. The convergence of the empirical independence score computed in this manner denoted as  $\Delta(\mathbf{t}, F|\hat{P})$ , to the population score,  $\Delta(\mathbf{t}, F|P)$ , is given by the following theorem.

Theorem 2. Let  $\mathcal{F} \coloneqq \{F \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k} : \| F \| \leq 1\}$ . Assume that  $\pmb{x} \sim \text{subgaussian}(\sigma)$ , i.e.,  $\forall \pmb{v} \in \mathbb{R}^k, \| \langle \pmb{v}, \pmb{x} \rangle \|_{\psi_2} \leq \sigma \| S^{\frac{1}{2}} \pmb{v} \|$ . Then  $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}^k$ $\| t \| = 1$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sup _ {F \in \mathcal {F}} | \Delta (\boldsymbol {t}, F | P) - \Delta (\boldsymbol {t}, F | \hat {P}) | \\ = O _ {P} \left(\sqrt {\frac {k \| S \| \operatorname* {m a x} (k , \sigma^ {4} \| S \|) \log n}{n}}\right) \\ \end{array}
$$

where  $\| .\|_{\psi_2}$  represents the subgaussian Orlicz norm.

The proof of this result is deferred to the Appendix section A.1.1.

It is important to note that the corrected independence score is not easy to optimize. In the noiseless case, whitening reduces the problem to one where the mixing matrix  $B$  is orthogonal, and this can be used to do efficient gradient descent in the Stiefel manifold of orthogonal matrices, as in [9]. However, this doesn't directly extend to optimizing the corrected score since the prewhitening matrix contains the covariance matrix of the Gaussian noise, making optimization hard unless the noise covariance is aligned with the signal covariance. Furthermore, while the independence score is defined for a given  $t$ , we take an average over  $t$  drawn uniformly from the  $d$  dimensional spherical Gaussian. Therefore, any iterative optimization method will require repeated estimation of this expectation at every gradient step. Therefore, instead of using this score directly as an optimization objective, we use this score to pick between different contrast functions after using each one of them to extract the demixing matrix. We call this the Meta algorithm (see Algorithm 1 for details). To gain an intuition of the independence score, we conduct an experiment where we use the dataset

mentioned in Section 6 (Figure 3b) and compute the independence score for  $B' = \epsilon B + (1 - \epsilon)I, \epsilon \in (0.5,1)$ . As we increase  $\epsilon$ ,  $B'$  approaches  $B$ , and hence the Amari error  $d_{B',B}$  (see Eq 8) decreases. We plot the variation of the independence score of  $B'$  against the Amari error in Figure 1 and note that even without the knowledge of the true  $B$ , the independence score can predict the quality of the solution accurately.

# 4 New Contrast Functions

In the introduction, we provided a discussion of individual shortcomings of different contrast functions. In this section, we present two new contrast functions based on the logarithm of the characteristic function (CHF) and the cumulant generating function (CGF). These do not depend on a particular cumulant, and the first only requires a finite second moment, which makes it suitable for heavy-tailed source signals. We will use  $f(\pmb{u} | P)$  or  $f(\pmb{u} | \pmb{x})$  where  $\pmb{x} \sim P$  interchangeably.

# CHF-based contrast function:

We will first present our characteristic function-based objective function. Recall that  $S$  denotes the covariance matrix of  $\mathbf{x}$ . We maximize the absolute value of following:

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (\boldsymbol {u} | P) = \log \mathbb {E} \exp (i \boldsymbol {u} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {x}) + \log \mathbb {E} \exp (- i \boldsymbol {u} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {x}) + \boldsymbol {u} ^ {T} S \boldsymbol {u} \\ = \log (\mathbb {E} \cos (\boldsymbol {u} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {x})) ^ {2} + \log (\mathbb {E} \sin (\boldsymbol {u} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {x})) ^ {2} + \boldsymbol {u} ^ {T} S \boldsymbol {u} \tag {4} \\ \end{array}
$$

![](images/800514c26453ec05756b278a825a9e2513aeb7e4f353fea82686b266871b3335.jpg)  
Figure 1: Correlation of independence score with Amari error between  $B' = \epsilon B + (1 - \epsilon)I$  and  $B$ , averaged over 10 random runs. The error bars represent standard deviations across runs.

The intuition is this is exactly zero for zero mean Gaussian data and maximizing this leads to extracting non-gaussian signal from the data. It also satisfies Assumption 1 a), b) and c). Now we show that the Hessian of this function evaluated at some  $\pmb{u}$  is, in fact, of the form  $BDB^{T}$  where  $D$  is some diagonal matrix.

Theorem 3. Consider the data generated from the noisy ICA model (Eq 1). Define  $f(\pmb{u}|P)$  as in Eq 4. We have  $\nabla^2 f(\pmb{u}|P) = BD_uB^T$ , for diagonal matrix  $D_{u}$ .

# CGF-based contrast function

The cumulant generating function also has similar properties (see [35] for the noiseless case). In this case, we maximize the absolute value of following:

$$
f (\boldsymbol {u} | P) = \log \mathbb {E} \exp \left(\boldsymbol {u} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {x}\right) - \frac {1}{2} \boldsymbol {u} ^ {T} S \boldsymbol {u} \tag {5}
$$

Like CHF, this vanishes iff  $\pmb{x}$  is mean zero Gaussian, and satisfies Assumption 1 a) and b). However, it cannot be expected to behave well in the heavy-tailed case. Finally, we show that the Hessian of this function evaluated at some  $\pmb{u}$  is, in fact, of the form  $BDB^{T}$  where  $D$  is some diagonal matrix.

Theorem 4. Consider the data generated from the noisy ICA model (Eq 1). Define  $f(\mathbf{u}|P)$  as in Eq 5. We have  $\nabla^2 f(\mathbf{u}|P) = BD_uB^T$ , for diagonal matrix  $D_{u}$ .

Proofs of Theorems 3 and 4 can be found in Appendix Section A.1. To estimate  $B$  using the contrast functions in Eq 4 and 5, we first estimate a  $C$  matrix, and then apply Algorithm 2 in [32].

# 5 Global and Local Convergence: Loss landscape of Noisy ICA

In this section, we present sufficient conditions for global and local convergence of a broad class of contrast functions. This covers the cumulant-based contrast functions and our CHF and CGF-based proposals.

# 5.1 Global Convergence

The classical proof of the global optima of the kurtosis or cumulant-based loss function was done by [14] in the non-noisy case. Here, the objective function is  $\max |\kappa_4(\pmb{x}^T\pmb{u})|$  s.t.  $\pmb{u}^{T}\pmb{u} = 1$ . The argument essentially uses that  $B$  is orthogonal (which is easy to do via whitening in the noiseless case) and transforms the loss function into one about  $\pmb{v} = B\pmb{u}$ . Since  $B$  is orthogonal, the norm constraint on  $\pmb{u}$  translates into a unit norm constraint on  $\pmb{v}$ . On the face of it, it seems that this should work in the noisy case due to properties 2 and 4 by simply optimizing over  $\pmb{v} = B\pmb{u}$  over potentially non-orthogonal mixing matrices  $B$ .

However, this leads to the issue that the norm constraint on the new  $\pmb{v}$  vector is no longer  $\pmb{v}^T\pmb{v} = 1$ , rendering the original argument invalid. In what follows, we will show that extending the earlier analysis of

the loss surface for the noiseless case to the noisy case is possible by introducing pseudo-euclidean constraints. Our framework includes a large family of contrast functions, including cumulants. To our knowledge, this is the first work to characterize the loss functions in the pseudo-euclidean space. In contrast, [33] provides global convergence of the cumulant-based methods by a convergence argument of the power method itself.

Consider the contrast function  $f(\boldsymbol{u}|P) \coloneqq \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{x} \sim P}\left[g(\boldsymbol{x}^T\boldsymbol{u})\right]$  and recall the definition of the quasi orthogonalization matrix  $C = BDB^{T}$ , where  $D$  is a diagonal matrix. For simplicity, WLOG let us assume that  $D$  is invertible. In this section, we aim to find the optimization objective that leads to the pseudo-Euclidean update in Eq 2. We will use  $\mathbb{E}$  to indicate integration over the distribution of  $\boldsymbol{x}$ , i.e.  $P$ . For  $f(C^{-1}\boldsymbol{u}|P) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{x} \sim P}\left[g(\boldsymbol{u}^T C^{-1}\boldsymbol{x})\right]$ , consider the following:

$$
\begin{array}{l} f \left(C ^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {u} | P\right) = \sum_ {i \in [ k ]} \mathbb {E} \left[ g \left(\frac {\left(B ^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {u}\right) _ {i}}{D _ {i i}} z _ {i}\right) \right] = \sum_ {i \in [ k ]} \mathbb {E} \left[ g \left(\alpha_ {i} \tilde {z} _ {i}\right) \right] \\ = \sum_ {i \in [ k ]} f \left(\frac {\alpha_ {i}}{D _ {i i}} \mid z _ {i}\right) \tag {6} \\ \end{array}
$$

where we define  $\pmb{\alpha} \coloneqq B^{-1}\pmb{u}$  and  $\tilde{z}_i = z_i / D_{ii}$ . We now propose to look at the loss function  $f(C^{-1}\pmb{u})$  subject to the "pseudo" norm constraint  $\pmb{u}^T C^{-1}\pmb{u} = 1$ . Note that the key difference is, we can, in fact, estimate a matrix of the form  $C = BDB^{T}$  from the data even when  $B$  is unknown. So our new objective is to optimize

$$
f \left(C ^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {u} | P\right) \text {s . t .} \boldsymbol {u} ^ {T} C ^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {u} = 1
$$

Note that optimizing this with a Lagrange multiplier, and setting the gradient of this to zero naturally gives us the direction  $\pmb{u} \propto \nabla f(C^{-1}\pmb{u})$ , which is the direction used in power method updates (Eq 2).

Furthermore, optimizing Eq 6 leads to the following transformed objective:

$$
\max  _ {\boldsymbol {\alpha}} \left| \sum_ {i} f \left(\frac {\alpha_ {i}}{D _ {i i}} \mid z _ {i}\right) \right| \quad \text {s . t .} \quad \sum_ {i} \frac {\alpha_ {i} ^ {2}}{D _ {i i}} = 1 \tag {7}
$$

Now we provide our theorem about maximizing  $f(C^{-1}\pmb{u}|P)$ . Analogous results hold for minimization.

Assumption 1. Consider any contrast function  $f$  defined for a mean zero random variable  $X$ . We assume

(a)  $f(u|X + Y) = f(u|X) + f(u|Y)$  for  $X \perp Y$  
(b)  $f(0|X) = 0, f'(0|X) = 0, h''(0|X) = 0$  
(c)  $f(u|G) = 0, \forall u$  for  $G \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$  
(d) The third derivative of  $f'''(u|X)$  does not change the sign in the half line  $[0, \infty)$  for the non-Gaussian random variable considered in the ICA problem.  
(e) WLOG,  $f(u|X) = f(-u|X)$  (symmetry)

We will use  $f^{\prime}(t_0|z_i)$  and  $f^{\prime \prime}(t_0|z_i)$  to denote  $\left.\frac{df(t|z_i)}{dt}\right|_{t = t_0}$  and  $\left.\frac{d^2f(t|z_i)}{dt^2}\right|_{t = t_0}$  respectively.

Theorem 5. Let  $C$  be a matrix of the form  $BDB^{T}$ , where  $d_{i} := D_{ii} = f^{\prime \prime}(u_{i}|z_{i})$  for some random  $u_{i}$ . Let  $S_{+} = \{i:d_{i} > 0\}$ . Consider a contrast function  $f:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$ . Assume that when applied to every non-Gaussian independent component Assumption 1 holds. Then  $f(C^{-1}\pmb {u}|\pmb {x})$  with the constraint of  $\langle \pmb {u},\pmb {u}\rangle_{C^{-1}} = 1$  has local maxima at  $B^{-1}\pmb {u} = \pmb {e}_i,i\in S_+$ . All solutions with  $e_i^T B^{-1}\pmb {u}\neq 0, \forall i$  are minima, and all solutions with  $e_i^T B^{-1}\pmb {u}\neq 0$  for  $1 < i < k$  are saddle points. These are the only fixed points.

Remark 1. Note that the above result immediately implies that for  $\tilde{C} = -C$ , the same optimization in Theorem 5 will have maxima at all  $\mathbf{u}$  such that  $B^{-1}\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{e}_i, i \in S_{-}$ .

Corollary 5.1.  $2k^{th}$  cumulant-based contrast functions for  $k > 1$ , have maxima and minima at the directions of the columns of  $B$ , as long as the independent components have a corresponding non-zero cumulant.

Proof. This is immediate since cumulants satisfy (a), (c). For (c) and (d) note that  $f(u|Z)$  is simply  $u^{2j}\kappa_{2j}(Z)$  where  $\kappa_{2j}(Z)$  is the  $2j^{th}$  cumulant of  $Z$ .

It is easy to extend our analysis to the case where  $C$  is not invertible; for the full proof, see the Appendix Section A.1. Condition (d) seems too strong, but it is not hard to construct examples of random variables  $Z$  where this fails for suitable contrast functions (see [25]). For such settings, it is hard to separate  $Z$  from a Gaussian. See the Appendix A.3.1 for more details.

# 5.2 Local Convergence

In this section, we establish a local convergence result for the power iteration-based method described in Eq 2. Define  $\forall t\in \mathbb{R},\forall i\in [d]$ , the functions  $q_{i}\left(t\right)\coloneqq f^{\prime}\left(\frac{\alpha_{i}}{D_{ii}}\Big|z_{i}\right)$ . Then, without loss of generality, we have the following result for the first corner:

Theorem 6. Let  $\pmb{\alpha}_i = B^{-1}\pmb{u}_i$  and  $\pmb{\alpha}^{*} \coloneqq B^{-1}\pmb{e}_{1}$ . Let contrast function,  $f(|X|)$ , satisfy assumptions 1 (a), (b), (c), and (e). Define  $c_{1}, c_{2}, c_{3} > 0$  as  $\forall i \in [d]$

1.  $\sup_{x\in [-\| B^{-1}\| _2,\| B^{-1}\| _2]}|q_i(x)|\leq c_1$  
2.  $\sup_{x\in [-\| B^{-1}\| _2,\| B^{-1}\| _2]}|q_i'(x)|\leq c_2$  
3.  $\sup_{x\in [-\| B^{-1}\| _2,\| B^{-1}\| _2]}|q_i^{\prime \prime}(x)|\leq c_3$

Define:

$$
\epsilon := \frac {\| B \| _ {F}}{\| B \pmb {e} _ {1} \| ^ {2}} \max \left\{\frac {c _ {3} + c _ {2} \| B \pmb {e} _ {1} \|}{| q _ {1} (\alpha_ {1} ^ {*}) |}, \frac {c _ {2} ^ {2}}{| q _ {1} (\alpha_ {1} ^ {*}) | ^ {2}}, \frac {c _ {3} \| B \pmb {e} _ {1} \|}{| q _ {1} ^ {\prime} (\alpha_ {1} ^ {*}) |} \right\}
$$

Let  $\| \pmb{\alpha}_0 - \pmb{\alpha}^*\|_2 \leq R$ ,  $R \leq \max \left\{\frac{c_2}{c_3}, \frac{1}{5\epsilon}\right\}$ . Then, we have  $\forall t \geq 1$ ,  $\frac{\|\pmb{\alpha}_{t+1} - \pmb{\alpha}^*\|}{\|\pmb{\alpha}_t - \pmb{\alpha}^*\|} \leq \frac{1}{2}$ .

Therefore, we can establish linear convergence without the third derivative constraint (Assumption 1 (d) mentioned in the case of global convergence), assuming some mild regularity conditions on the contrast functional and a close enough initialization. The proof is included in Appendix Section A.1.2.

# 6 Experiments

In this section, we provide experiments to compare the fixed-point algorithms based on the characteristic function (CHF), the cumulant generating function (CGF) (Eqs 4 and 5) with the kurtosis-based algorithm (PEGI- $\kappa_4$  [32]). We also compare against noiseless ICA $^1$  algorithms - FastICA, JADE, and PFICA. These six algorithms are included as candidates for the Meta algorithm (see Algorithm 1). We also present the Uncorrected Meta or Unc. Meta to denote the Meta algorithm with the uncorrected independence score proposed in CHFICA [16].

Experimental setup: Similar to [32], the mixing matrix  $B$  is constructed as  $B = U\Lambda V^T$ , where  $U, V$  are  $k$  dimensional random orthonormal matrices, and  $\Lambda$  is a diagonal matrix with  $\Lambda_{ii} \in [1, 3]$ . The covariance matrix  $\Sigma$  of the noise  $\pmb{g}$  follows the Wishart distribution and is chosen to be  $\frac{\rho}{k} R R^T$ , where  $k$  is the number of sources, and  $R$  is a random Gaussian matrix. Higher values of the noise power  $\rho$  can make the noisy ICA problem harder. Keeping  $B$  fixed, we report the median of 100 random runs of data generated from a given distribution (different for different experiments). The quasi-orthogonalization matrix for CHF and CGF is initialized as  $\hat{B}\hat{B}^T$  using the mixing matrix,  $\hat{B}$ , estimated via PFICA. The performance of CHF and CGF is based on a single random initialization.

# 7 Conclusion

ICA is a classical problem that aims to extract independent non-Gaussian components. The vast literature on both noiseless and noisy ICA introduces many different inference methods based on a variety of contrast functions for separating the non-Gaussian signal from the Gaussian noise. Each has its own set of shortcomings. We aim to identify the best method for a given dataset in a data-driven fashion. In this paper, we propose a nonparametric score, which is used to evaluate the quality of the solution of any inference method for the noisy ICA model. Using this score, we design a Meta algorithm, which chooses among a set of candidate solutions of the demixing matrix. We also provide new contrast functions and a computationally efficient optimization framework. While they also have shortcomings, we show that our diagnostic can remedy them. We provide uniform convergence properties of our score and theoretical results for local and global convergence of our methods. On a variety of simulated experiments we show that while different methods shine under different distributional settings, our Meta algorithm can achieve the accuracy of the best candidate.
